topics.title: Rai: stone money across the sea
topics.subtitle: Quarry rights, skilled work, canoes, ships and recognized obligations
topics.description: A twelve-chapter journey from Palauan quarries to Yapese village life, with named voyages and the later changes brought by commercial shipping.
topics.method: Archaeological contexts, oral traditions, historical descriptions and named shipping records answer different questions. The movie does not invent a first rai year, an exact prehistoric canoe, or a uniform price system. Related places and voyages also belong to the master atlas.
topics.dateNote: A scene year is a viewing position, not a new historical claim. Unplaced evidence retains its uncertain date; a line is a schematic connection, not a recovered sailing track.

scenes.title: The caves had earlier lives
scenes.body: Begin in Palau, long before the dated ship cargoes. Chelechol ra Orrak preserves an early cemetery, while Ulong has early occupation evidence. These are Palauan histories. Later Yapese quarrying reused some places and disturbed earlier deposits, so an ancient bone or charcoal date beneath quarry debris does not automatically date stone money. The opening chapter establishes the landscape and the evidence problem before introducing the trade.
scenes.note: c.3000 cal BP is a rounded archaeological age, not a first-rai date.

scenes.title: First arrange the right to work
scenes.body: Yapese quarry workers entered places held by Palauan communities. Access depended on relationships, gifts and agreements; it was not a matter of finding an unclaimed cliff. Food, beads and labor could matter within those negotiations. The contrast between coastal and inland quarries also meant different work and transport problems. Named places on this map preserve that geography without pretending they all began producing stones in the same year.
scenes.note: 1725 is a viewing point in the approximate Metuker onset window. Undated quarries retain their uncertain chronology.

scenes.title: Make a disk that can survive movement
scenes.body: Working a rai involved selecting stone, establishing the outline, shaping the body, drilling a central opening and finishing the surfaces. Unfinished disks expose stages that a completed object conceals. Iron blades at Metuker provide direct evidence for tools within a quarry context; earlier techniques are reconstructed partly from historical and oral accounts. A hole did more than create the recognizable form: it enabled a timber to help carry or support the load. Breakage could interrupt the whole investment.
scenes.note: Manufacturing is a reconstructed sequence, not one dated workshop demonstration.

scenes.title: A quarry is also a place to live and eat
scenes.body: Workers needed food while they shaped stone and prepared it for movement. Shellfish remains at Omis and Metuker connect the expedition to surrounding marine habitats. Differences between these assemblages may reflect access and choices, but also disposal, crushing and the movement of soil during quarry work. Stone platforms and alignments show investment in the working landscape. The labor of sustaining an expedition belongs beside the dramatic image of carrying a giant disk.
scenes.note: The viewing year supplies context only. Quarry-food assemblages are not dated to a single meal or expedition.

scenes.title: Small valuables travelled into the same quarry world
scenes.body: Glass beads at Chelechol ra Orrak connect the local exchange network with manufacturers far beyond Micronesia. Analysis identifies many as Bohemian products made around 1830–1850. Their date tells us when those objects could begin their journey, not exactly when workers brought them to Palau. Beads had their own categories and histories of value. Pairing them with rai shows that the quarry relationship involved several kinds of valuables, each interpreted by people within their own social practices.
scenes.note: 1840 is a viewing point inside the bead manufacture range. The marker is the later findsite, not a dated 1840 deposition.

scenes.title: The sea crossing starts at the landing place
scenes.body: A finished stone still had to reach the water, be loaded and survive an ocean crossing. Accounts describe canoes and rafts, with timbers through stone perforations helping support the load. At Omis a tidal dock has been interpreted as a way to load before rising water floated a raft. Specialist navigators and suitable weather remained essential. The line across the sea represents a connection; it does not recreate wind choices, intermediate stops or the precise way a particular stone was secured.
scenes.note: Cheyne’s documented 1843 delivery anchors this chapter’s map. The canoe arrangements come from later nineteenth-century accounts, including Le Hunte in 1883; they do not reconstruct his ship’s cargo rig. Tidal loading is an archaeological interpretation.

scenes.title: One recorded stone, a specific relationship
scenes.body: Cheyne’s journal records a perforated stone gift from a Palauan chief delivered to Yapese leaders on 23 August 1843. The episode makes an exchange visible through a particular witness. It should not be promoted into the origin of rai, nor treated as a complete description of its social uses. Historical records can identify participants and occasions with unusual clarity while still reflecting the observer’s vocabulary and limited understanding.
scenes.note: The date belongs to the journaled delivery. The endpoints remain regional.

scenes.title: A stone’s place and its owner can differ
scenes.body: Once on Yap, a disk could stand beside a path, house or ceremonial ground while its recognized ownership changed. Mangyol and Baleyrach illustrate a village setting in which stone money, gathering spaces and chiefly places were connected. The familiar word bank should not make us imagine a modern bank building. Transfers involved relationships and obligations, and value could depend on remembered work and circumstances as well as visible size or finish. Rai existed among other valuables and activities.
scenes.note: The map follows the documented return aboard Vesta in 1865. The explanation of ownership and obligations draws on later accounts; it does not date Mangyol’s foundation or claim that all stones had the same uses.

scenes.title: Foreign transport was already part of the network
scenes.body: Tetens recorded ten Yapese returning aboard Vesta with stones they had cut in Palau. The passengers and their work remain central: a foreign ship joined an existing production relationship. This documented voyage predates O’Keefe’s operation and prevents the entire technological change being credited to one later merchant. It also shows why ship capacity and access could affect who traveled, which loads returned and how obligations were negotiated.
scenes.note: Late 1865 is the cited journal placement; no exact sailing day or unsupported cargo tonnage is added.

scenes.title: Copra, ships and a commercial base
scenes.body: O’Keefe’s ships began carrying Yapese to Palau in 1872. The arrangements linked transport with copra labor and markets beyond the islands. Taraang was a household and a workplace as well as a trading headquarters, with warehouses, waterfront facilities and workers of varied origins. These changes increased commercial possibilities while depending on Yapese choices and Palauan access. They transformed parts of an existing system rather than creating the value of stone from nothing.
scenes.note: 1872 marks this operator’s involvement and the start of his documented Taraang tenure.

scenes.title: A named cargo reveals the changed scale
scenes.body: Swan returned to Yap from Palau on 1 February 1884 with a reported 1,480 pieces of stone money. The number makes large-scale shipping tangible, but the stones’ individual sizes are unspecified and total tonnage cannot be calculated. More efficient manufacture and transport did not make all stones equivalent. Earlier stones could retain value associated with difficult voyages and remembered histories. Production cost, physical appearance and social valuation need to be considered together.
scenes.note: Cargo count is documentary reporting, not an archaeological measurement of every piece.

scenes.title: Keep the society in the story
scenes.body: A reported German order in 1899 tried to halt Palauan quarrying, linking commercial rivalry with demands for labor on Yap. Later carriage of stones warns against treating the order as an immediate end. Colonial government, mission work and cable networks added other forms of outside power; Japanese seizure followed in 1914. None is a date when Indigenous knowledge or obligations simply disappeared. Reading rai as only a lesson about modern currency removes the quarry rights, navigators, workers and changing political relationships that made its history.
scenes.note: The narrative stops before the atlas cutoff of 1934. The cutoff is not an end date for rai or Yapese society.
